must_remember: In antiferromagnetic materials, adjacent magnetic moments are coupled via an exchange interaction that favors antiparallel alignment due to the negative sign of the exchange integral ($J < 0$).
The critical temperature below which antiferromagnetic ordering occurs is known as the Néel temperature ($T_N$).
Below $T_N$, the magnetic susceptibility ($chi$) decreases with decreasing temperature, reaching zero at $0\text{ K}$ for parallel susceptibility.
Above $T_N$, antiferromagnetic materials follow the modified Curie-Weiss law given by $\chi = \frac{C}{T + \theta}$, where $\theta$ is the paramagnetic Curie temperature.
Classic examples of antiferromagnetic materials include Manganese oxide ($	ext{MnO}$), Nickel oxide ($	ext{NiO}$), and Chromium ($	ext{Cr}$).
Antiferromagnets exhibit zero net spontaneous macroscopic magnetization because the two interpenetrating sub-lattices ($M_A$ and $M_B$) have equal and opposite magnetization vectors.

glossary.meaning: The critical temperature above which an antiferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic.
A quantum mechanical parameter that determines the coupling between adjacent spins; negative for antiferromagnetism.
A constant appearing in the modified Curie-Weiss law for antiferromagnetic materials above $T_N$.
The net magnetization vectors of the two interpenetrating sub-lattices into which an antiferromagnetic crystal is divided.
The relation $\chi = \frac{C}{T + \theta}$ governing magnetic susceptibility in the paramagnetic region above $T_N$.
